line: Morning. I'm Walt. I'm at this table most days till noon, waiting on {chessRival}. You play?
A little. That's what {chessRival} said the first time, and he took my rook in nine moves. White or black?
choice2: Maybe I'll just watch for now.

line: Suit yourself. Stand on that side, you'll have the sun behind you. He's late. Wednesdays he takes his grandson to school first.
choice2: Do you come here every day?
choice3: I'll let you wait for him.

line: {chessRival}? Retired, like me. He's been beating me at this table three years now. I still couldn't tell you his last name.
choice1: Three years, and you never asked?
choice3: I'll catch you both another time.

line: _moves a pawn forward and back_ The first year we didn't say ten words. His English was worse then, and I'm not a talker. You don't need much for this. Check, mate, your move.
choice1: Did you ever ask where he's from?
choice3: I'll let you get set up.

line: Second year. He told me about his town, the river, his school. I told him I'd never been further than Ohio. He thought that was the funniest thing he'd ever heard. $ [warm] Last winter I had the flu two weeks. He's the one who came by with soup. Not my daughter. Him.
choice2: I'll let you wait for him.

line: Most days. I live two blocks that way, same house since 1979. My wife picked it. The block's mostly new people now. Kids on bikes again, which is nice.
choice3: I'll let you get back to the board.

line: Some. The family next door brings my trash cans in when I forget. I couldn't say their names right if you paid me, so I wave a lot. They wave back.
choice1: Have you ever asked them to say it again?

line: Once. The mother said it twice, slow, and I still got it wrong, and we both stood there. I didn't want to make her do it a third time. _shrugs_ So I wave.
choice1: Maybe she wouldn't mind a third time.

line: Pawn to e4. {chessRival}'s late, so you've got his seat till he shows. Your move. Don't take all day.
Book move. Fine. You live around here, or just cutting through the park?
choice1: I live on Grand, near the library.

line: Huh, {chessRival} does that. You self-taught?
choice1: Mostly. Phone apps and a lot of losing.
choice2: My dad taught me, back when we lived on Grand.
choice3: I should go. Good game so far.

line: _studies the board_ It shows. That's not an insult. You live around here, or just cutting through the park?
choice1: I live on Grand, near the library.
choice3: I should go. Good game so far.

line: Grand. Our dentist was up there, right next to the bakery. My wife'd always buy some bread after an appointment. Shame it's gone, she'd have hated that. $ _moves his queen_ Check, by the way.
choice3: I should head out. Thanks for the game.

line: June. She passed, three winters ago. She'd have liked you, you don't talk during the move. _taps the board_ You're still in check.
choice2: Do you miss how Grand used to be?
choice3: I should head out. I'm sorry about June.

line: Some of it. The bakery, sure. The new guy on that corner opens at six. Makes some strange breads, no label I can read. Can't get used to those. But he always remembers what coffee I like. $ [warm] ...and sneaks me a strange pastry once in a while.
choice1: Any of them you've gotten used to?
choice2: I should head out. Thanks for the game.
choice3: I get the one called {homeBread} sometimes.

line: _thinks about it_ One. Round, with something sweet in the middle. I don't ask what it's called. $ I don't read half the signs on Grand anymore, and that bothers me some mornings. Then he says 'the usual, Walt,' and it doesn't. Your move.
The {homeBread}? Say it again. _says it under his breath, twice_ Maybe I'll point at that one tomorrow, see if he laughs. $ Your move. You're still in check.
choice3: I should head out. Thanks for the game.

line: Bishop. Sure. Here comes {chessRival}, walking like he owns the park. You want to keep the seat, or watch him beat me properly?
choice2: Let him have it. I should go.

line: Smart. {chessRival}, this is {playerName}, from Grand. Don't go easy, they'll get soft.
Morning, {playerName}. {chessRival}'s late again. You want his seat till he shows?
_sets up the pieces_ You're white, same as last time. Don't open with the knight. {chessRival} does that and I'm sick of it.
Hm. {chessRival} showed me a trap last month, with the bishop. Took me three Wednesdays to see what he did. You want to see it?
Here, and here, and the queen's got nowhere to go. He says that's how the old men played in the park where he grew up. Money on it, too. We don't do money.
choice1: Did he play a lot, back then?

line: Every day after school, he says, with his uncle. He talks about that uncle more than anybody. I think this table's a bit of that for him. I don't ask.
choice1: Maybe it's that for you too.

line: Lost four straight to {chessRival}. He's started bringing his grandson to watch, which doesn't help.
choice3: I'll let you get your revenge.

line: Nine, ten. He translates when the trash talk gets complicated. I think he makes some of it up.
choice1: What did he say last time?
choice2: I'll let you get your revenge.

line: 'My grandfather says you play like a man waiting for a bus.' Fair. I've been waiting for the 14 since 1979. $ The kid said it in English and then said something to his grandpa, and they both laughed. I didn't ask for that half.
choice2: He sounds like a good kid.

line: You're out here more than the pigeons. {chessRival} wants a rematch, by the way. Says you got lucky.
A little. You don't castle soon enough. He used to do the same, the first year. He got better.
choice1: He's played here since he got here?

line: Near enough. He told me once this table was the first place in the city nobody asked him for a form. Just white or black. I didn't know what to say to that, so I said white.
Board's taken.
choice1: Fair. I was rude last time.

line: Huh. Okay. Sit, if you want. Don't touch the clock.
There you are. You got a minute? I want to ask you something, and it's not about chess.
My granddaughter has a school project. 'Interview someone who came here from somewhere else.' She wants to interview {chessRival}. I said I'd ask him. Then I realised I don't know how to ask.
Straight. Sure. Thing is, he might not want to tell a kid with a clipboard all of it. I wouldn't. What do you think he'd say?
choice2: Ask him what he'd want her to know.
choice3: I'd better not guess. See you, Walt.

line: Thirty-one years at the plant, I worked next to a guy from the Philippines. Teddy. Taught me the Sicilian on lunch breaks. I never once asked him how he got here. $ [guarded] He died in 2009. I went to the funeral and found out more in an hour than in twenty years.
choice2: That's a hard way to find out.

line: Afternoon. I went for a haircut and got a speech instead.
On the TV over the mirror. Whole shop nodding along. Sal asked me what I thought and I said I came in for a trim.
choice2: I get not wanting to get into it.

line: I think rules are rules. I also think {chessRival} didn't come to the park this week, first time in three years. _looks at the empty seat_ I don't like the two of those together.
I don't have his number. Three years. I know how he takes his coffee and which bishop he's going to throw away. But I never asked his number.
Maybe. I've never been in there. I'd feel like I was walking into somebody's kitchen. $ [neutral] You go there, right? If you see him, tell him the board's still here.
choice3: I'll see what I can do.

line: My daughter called last night, all lit up about the new president. I told her I'll get excited when the 14 bus runs on time.
Something about the backlog. People waiting ten years for their papers. She works at the county, she sees the files. I didn't know it took ten years.
Yeah. My grandfather got off a boat and was a citizen in five. I figured that's how it still worked. Shows what I know.
choice1: Did he keep anything from back there?

line: Card games and a temper. Not the language, my dad wouldn't have it in the house. I've got one recipe card in his writing that I can't read. It's on the fridge.
choice2: That's a good thing to keep.

line: {chessRival} says you've been at {homeCenter} a lot.
choice1: I have. Is that a problem?

line: No problem. He says the {centerDrink}'s better there than at the stand by the gate. I told him {centerDrink} is {centerDrink}.
choice3: I'll let you get back to it.

line: That's what he said. He also said I could come by Saturday, if I wanted. I said I'd think about it.
Probably not. Not because of anything. I'm seventy-four and I go to four places, and I like the four places. $ [warm] But he's asked twice now. When {chessRival} asks twice he means it.
Morning. If you're waiting on the paper, it'll be a while. I'm Walt. I'm about a quarter through.
choice1: I'm {playerName}. I'll take the front page when you're done.

line: Here, I'm done with the front. They stopped delivering to my block in March. Twenty-six years I had the Ledger on my step.
choice2: Twenty-six years is a long time.
choice3: Thanks. Enjoy the rest of it.

line: Not enough of us left on the block who take it, they said. Half the houses on my street changed hands in ten years. Nice people. They read it on their phones.
choice1: Do you know the new neighbours?

line: Same paper, a day late, and somebody's done the crossword in pen. I know who. I won't say. _turns the page_ They moved the obituaries, too. I read those first now, at my age.
Walt lowers the paper an inch. "They moved the crossword to page nine. Nobody asked me."
choice1: Want a second pair of eyes on it?

line: Fine. Seventeen across, 'Old meeting place,' five letters. Starts with an A.
Agora. Huh. My granddaughter would have had that in two seconds. She's eleven and she corrects my English, which did fine for seventy years.
I say 'warsh' for wash. Everybody did, where I grew up. She says nobody talks like that anymore. $ [warm] Maybe not. My wife did. I'm keeping it.
You're in here as much as me lately. Dana asked if you were my grandkid. I told her my grandkids don't read the obituaries.
choice1: Anybody we know in them today?

line: Nobody I knew. A woman who ran the shoe repair on Grand for forty years. Her kids wrote a long piece, in two languages. I read the English half and looked at the other half a while.
choice2: That's a nice thing for them to do.

line: Everybody did. She fixed my work boots for thirty years. I never knew her first name till this morning. _folds the paper_ You'd think you'd ask, in thirty years. Now I can't even ask her how to pronounce it.
Don't take that chair, the spring's gone. I'm Walt. They called forty-one twenty minutes ago, and I'm forty-six. Take a number, you're in for quite a wait.
Blood pressure, every three months, so my daughter stops calling. It's always fine. They take it twice anyway, like they don't believe the first one.
choice1: Mine goes up just sitting here.

line: Mondays, yes. Five people working here and a waiting room for thirty. The nurse with the braid does the front desk and the shots both.
After six years, sort of. Half the room's from somewhere else now. She does those patients with an interpreter on the phone, on speaker. Takes a while. Nobody complains, much.

I mind the chairs. The wait, no. _glances around the room_ The lady next to me last time had her daughter on the phone, telling her what the doctor said. If it was me over there, I'd want somebody on the phone too.
You sick, or just keeping me company? They've got the cooking channel on again.
Nobody in this room is allowed to eat any of it. Salt, butter, the works. Last week a man made bread on there and the whole room went quiet.
Eggs. Since my wife passed, eggs and soup from a can. {chessRival} brought me something in a container this winter. I don't know what it was. I ate all of it.
choice1: Did you ask him what it was?

line: Next day. He told me the name, and I said it back wrong, and he laughed a full minute. I still can't say it. I ask for 'the thing from January' and he knows.
choice1: That's a good name for it.

line: Walt sees you, and goes back to his paper.
choice1: Sorry I was rude last time, Walt.

line: Hm. All right. Here, you can have the sports section. I don't read it anyway.
Not now. I'm thinking. Ask me after this move.
Walt lowers the paper an inch. "Somebody left a flyer in the sports section again. Potluck, Thursday."
_hands it over_ Five languages and a drawing of a casserole. That's Ruth, the library woman. She puts one in every paper in this room. I've had eleven.

Went once, after June passed. Ruth sat me between a man who fixes elevators and a girl doing her homework. $ Everybody on this side of town does what Ruth says, me included, apparently. I had seconds. I haven't been back. Not because of her.
Too many people being glad to see me. _folds the paper_ My wife was the one who went to things. I'm better with one person and a board.
choice1: One person and a board is a start.

line: Walt lowers the paper an inch. "Frank DeLuca's in the business section. Again."
Hardware store on Fifth. 'Local merchant hosts small-business breakfast.' Bagels. He's in here more than the mayor. Half of Fifth won't change a lightbulb without asking Frank which one.

I like him fine. He's sold me the same washer for thirty years and never charged me twice. $ [guarded] He told {chessRival} once to 'practise his English on the customers.' {chessRival} didn't go back for a month. Frank never noticed. That's Frank.
No. I'm not a talker. Next time {chessRival} needed bolts I went along and did the asking. Frank gave us the good ones.
choice1: That was a good thing to do.

line: Ruth from the library came by the tables. Wants a chess night in the basement. Me and {chessRival}, teaching.
choice3: Tell me later. I'll let you play.

line: I said I'm not a teacher. She said I've taught {chessRival} every bad habit he has. Can't argue. $ She gets her way. Everybody on this side of town ends up doing one thing for Ruth.
Chess night, apparently. Thursdays. {chessRival} wants to bring the board from his uncle. Ruth's doing the flyer in his language and mine. I told her mine's mostly 'check.'
Frank DeLuca came by the tables. Wants the Hornets' end-of-season picnic here Saturday, and the chess tables for the parents.
His tables, the way he talks. He asked the park office, and the park office said whatever Frank wants. Nobody on Fifth says no to Frank. He means it nice. He brought donuts.
I said {chessRival} and me will be here at nine like always. He said good, we can teach the kids. 'In English, though, so the parents can follow.' $ {chessRival} said he'd teach them in chess.
